Finley & Basu (paper paywalled; read via the university release) find permanent restrictions barely move average summer use except in visible drought, implying the effective unenforced response is small in normal years; Fresno RCT shows near-perfect detection only cut violations 17%, so many households did not comply even under enforcement-as-usual. extra_sources.title: Impacts of Water Development on Great Salt Lake and the Wasatch Front
extra_sources.quote: water diversions ... represent a persistent reduction in water supply to the lake, decreasing its elevation by 11 feet

arithmetic: Basin-average share of supply reaching the lake ~ 1,665 / (1,665 + 2,320) = 0.42 (inflow 2000-2025, depletions 1989-2024; periods differ). Statewide seeded increment 180-200 KAF x 0.35 = 63-70 KAF to the lake.
notes: Assumption. No source gives a delivery share for seeded runoff. Basin water budget implies ~40% of total supply reaches the lake on average; seeded water arrives in spring runoff in headwaters above most storage and diversions, so marginal delivery could be lower in dry years (reservoirs capture it) or higher in wet years (spill). 0.35 is near the basin average and the 0.2-0.6 range covers it. Note the DWR 180-200 KAF figure is statewide, not GSL-basin only.

arithmetic: Utah portion: sprinkler/pivot upgrades 6 + 10 = 16 KAF (<$210/AF); + wheel-line to SDI 21 = 37 KAF (<$510/AF); surface to SDI 8.7% x 830 KAF = 72 KAF (>= $1,014/AF). Whole basin irrigation-only strategy reaches 132.6 KAF at $563/AF on 370,543 acres (Table 5-2).
notes: Assumption. 70 KAF sits inside the published technical potential but requires the expensive surface-to-SDI conversions (>$1,000/AF), inconsistent with the model's $581/AF cost midpoint; at costs <= ~$670/AF the Utah ceiling is ~37 KAF (basin ~132 KAF). Realised programme performance is far lower (1,500 AF depletion from 11,000 acres, 2019-23). Suggest range 15-110 and consider ~40 as central if cost stays at $581.

arithmetic: All-aggressive-policy potential by 2065: statewide 240->171 gpcd = -29%; Salt Lake 210->161 = -23%; Weber 250->167 = -33%; Bear River 304->212 = -30%; Provo 222->148 = -33%.
notes: Assumption. The state's own technical maximum with every aggressive policy, over 50 years, is ~23-33% of M&I use. Because depletion is concentrated outdoors (91% of outdoor use depleted) and outdoor is where cuts concentrate, a depletion cap can exceed the use cap, so 0.4 is at the upper edge of what is published, not clearly wrong. A charge alone (RFF) delivers less than the full policy package. EPA conservation-guidelines page gave no number; DWR water-use reporting page gave none. A central value near 0.3 would be better supported; kept as evidence (cautious).

arithmetic: Foregone return = WTA $355 - $50 leasing cost = $305/acre. Check: yield x $212/ton - operating cost (Table B-5): 4-cut flood 4.24x212-608.78 = 290; 4-cut wheel 320; 4-cut pivot 443; 2-cut flood 62; 2-cut wheel 74; 2-cut pivot 136; acreage-weighted (Table B-2) = $304.5/acre.
notes: The model cites NASS Utah, whose landing page has no net-return figure. The 2026 DWR/USU analysis gives ~$305/acre returns over operating costs (2023 dollars, 25-yr average price $212/ton), range ~$62 (2-cut flood) to ~$443 (4-cut pivot). This excludes ownership costs (stand establishment, depreciation, land), so a full-cost net return would be lower; if the model means returns after all costs, 175 could be defensible but is unsourced. For a levy weighed against what a farmer gives up in the short run, $305 is the better-sourced figure.
